entries.topicDescription: Persisting preferences and files safely: DataStore, app-specific storage, scoped storage, and backups.

tips.title: Prefer DataStore over SharedPreferences for new code
tips.content:
DataStore stores small pieces of data asynchronously with coroutines and Flow. Reads come back as a Flow that re-emits when the data changes, and writes happen in a transaction on a background dispatcher — so it can't block the main thread the way SharedPreferences can (for example when it flushes to disk in the middle of a lifecycle callback).

Preferences DataStore holds key-value pairs, similar to SharedPreferences but with a safe API. It does not encrypt anything: for secrets, protect the values with a Keystore-backed key as well.

tips.title: Create exactly one DataStore instance per file
tips.content:
DataStore assumes it is the only writer of its file in the process. Creating a second instance for the same file makes it throw an IllegalStateException ("There are multiple DataStores active for the same file") as soon as both are active.

Declare the property delegate once at the top level of a Kotlin file (the delegate keeps a single instance per Context), or provide the instance from your DI container as a singleton. Never build a DataStore inside a function that can run more than once.

tips.title: Migrate from SharedPreferences with SharedPreferencesMigration
tips.content:
Moving an existing app to DataStore doesn't have to lose saved settings. Pass a SharedPreferencesMigration when you create the DataStore: before the first read or write, DataStore copies the old values across and then cleans up the migrated keys from SharedPreferences.

The migration runs once and is safe to keep in the code across releases; after every user has migrated it simply does nothing.

tips.title: Handle read errors, and rely on edit being atomic
tips.content:
DataStore reports problems reading the file as an IOException on the data Flow. Catch it and fall back to defaults so one bad read doesn't crash collectors, and rethrow anything else.

Writes are transactional: everything you change inside one edit block is applied together or not at all. Group related changes in a single edit rather than several separate ones, so readers never observe a half-updated state.

tips.title: Proto DataStore stores typed objects instead of loose keys
tips.content:
Preferences DataStore is untyped: keys and types are only checked by convention. Typed DataStore persists a whole object through a Serializer you provide, giving you a real schema with defaults. It works with Protocol Buffers, or with kotlinx.serialization as below.

Throw CorruptionException when the stored bytes can't be read so DataStore can apply your corruption handler instead of crashing, and remember that the object is immutable — update it with updateData and copy().

tips.title: Know which storage directory fits the data
tips.content:
Each app has private directories that need no permission. filesDir holds durable private files and is included in backups; cacheDir holds data you can rebuild, and the system may delete it when storage runs low; noBackupFilesDir is private and excluded from backups; getExternalFilesDir() is app-specific space on shared storage that other apps can technically read, and it is removed when the app is uninstalled.

Pick by what happens if the data disappears: rebuildable data goes in cacheDir, must-keep private data in filesDir, and device-specific or secret data in noBackupFilesDir.
tips.codeSnippet:
val documents = File(context.filesDir, "documents")      // durable + backed up
val thumbnails = File(context.cacheDir, "thumbnails")    // may be cleared by the system
val deviceKey = File(context.noBackupFilesDir, "key")    // private, never backed up
val exports = context.getExternalFilesDir("exports")     // app-specific on shared storage

tips.title: Use the Photo Picker instead of broad media permissions
tips.content:
Scoped storage (enforced from Android 11) stops apps from freely browsing shared storage. To let users pick photos or videos you don't need any storage permission at all: the system Photo Picker returns a content URI for just the items the user selects.

Reading all of a user's media with READ_MEDIA_IMAGES / READ_MEDIA_VIDEO (Android 13+) is only justified for gallery-style apps; for "attach a photo" flows, the picker is simpler and safer, and it is backported to older devices through Google Play services.

tips.title: Let the user choose files with the Storage Access Framework
tips.content:
For documents, exports, and backups, the Storage Access Framework lets the user pick or create a file anywhere (device storage or cloud providers) and hands your app a URI, again with no storage permission. Use CreateDocument to save and OpenDocument to read.

Access to a picked URI ends when your process dies unless you call takePersistableUriPermission; do that if you need to reopen the same file later, and store the URI string.

tips.title: Exclude device-bound data from backups
tips.content:
Auto Backup copies an app's files, databases and SharedPreferences to the user's cloud backup and restores them on a new device by default. Data that is tied to the device, like tokens or files encrypted with a Keystore key, is useless after a restore because Keystore keys are not backed up, and code that tries to decrypt it will fail.

On Android 12+ declare rules in a data-extraction-rules file (separate sections for cloud backup and device-to-device transfer) via android:dataExtractionRules, and keep android:fullBackupContent for Android 11 and lower.
tips.codeSnippet:
<!-- AndroidManifest.xml -->
<application
    android:dataExtractionRules="@xml/data_extraction_rules"
    android:fullBackupContent="@xml/backup_rules" />

<!-- res/xml/data_extraction_rules.xml -->
<data-extraction-rules>
    <cloud-backup>
        <exclude domain="sharedpref" path="secure_prefs.xml" />
        <exclude domain="database" path="session_cache.db" />
    </cloud-backup>
    <device-transfer>
        <exclude domain="sharedpref" path="secure_prefs.xml" />
    </device-transfer>
</data-extraction-rules>
